locator.quote: A quantum algorithm decodes an address cheaply and finds the winning column in about $\sqrt m$ queries.

feedback.feedback: The square-root summary is accurate at the level of the leading power for fixed k, but neither the fixed-parameter convention nor the suppressed logarithms is visible in this sentence. Later the same paper varies k and pays an exponential decoder cost. The abstract makes these two regimes look closer than they are.
feedback.why_it_matters: A reader scanning only the abstract can mistake the square-root mechanism for a bound uniform in the Forrelation parameter.
feedback.advice: Qualify this one cost summary by fixed k and suppressed logarithms. Keep the detailed constant out of the abstract.

locator.quote: exact certificate tests complete the algorithm on every input.

feedback.feedback: The tests themselves are exact; searching for a failing test is bounded error. This last sentence is susceptible to the reading that the final certificate verification is exact, even though §3.3 correctly explains that a false candidate can be accepted by missing a defect.
feedback.why_it_matters: The distinction matters to the total decision guarantee and to what “finds the winning column” promises.
feedback.advice: Name bounded-error search over exact local tests at this first occurrence. This is a wording repair, not an error in the algorithm.

locator.quote: Its central feature is that a true certificate can defeat every rival in a cheap comparison

feedback.feedback: This is the right organizing observation for a quantum referee. It names the unusual guarantee before invoking tournament machinery and explains why promise violations in a rival are part of the construction rather than an exceptional case.
feedback.why_it_matters: The reader can now ask the useful question: how does winner-only reliability suffice for coherent search?
feedback.advice: Preserve this mechanism-led opening when shortening the history.

locator.quote: The exponent six and coefficient $1/400$ are explicit choices in this reconstruction.

feedback.feedback: The theorem is credited to OpenAI while the displayed quantitative choices are assigned to the reconstruction immediately afterward. This prevents the more explicit statement from quietly transferring authorship of the separation.
feedback.why_it_matters: The constant choices and the original separation are different contributions; this sentence makes their relationship recoverable.
feedback.advice: Keep the sentence adjacent to Theorem 1.

locator.quote: The same circuit defines the function in both bounds of (2).

feedback.feedback: This short sentence protects a real mathematical issue: a transcript-defined total function depends on its circuit witness, so two independently existential circuits would not by themselves give a separating family.
feedback.why_it_matters: It lets the referee check the quantum and classical arguments against one total function.
feedback.advice: Retain the sentence and the corresponding construction paragraph. This repetition is functional rather than filler.

locator.quote: Grover search for OR and its matching lower bound give the basic quadratic separation.

feedback.feedback: The paragraph restarts the chronology after the previous paragraph has already walked through the 5/2, 8/3 and near-cubic exponents with the composition calculation. The calculation is useful; the second parade of the same exponents feels like a second introduction to it.
feedback.why_it_matters: The quantum mechanism arrives later because the reader traverses the same historical progression twice.
feedback.advice: Keep one compact chronology and the AND–OR cost calculation, but avoid repeating every milestone in prose immediately after explaining it.

feedback.feedback: The exact factor 20 arrives in the conceptual overview before the reader knows that it buys a union bound over possible cell queries. At this point the important fact is that the address has logarithmic length.
feedback.why_it_matters: The first pass asks the reader to retain a numerical design choice that has no current explanatory job.
feedback.advice: Use a logarithmic address length in the overview and introduce the exact factor at the formal definition, where its purpose is already stated.

locator.quote: uses these probabilities as weights to produce a short list

feedback.feedback: The actual weights are products of comparison probabilities against all previous pivots, not individual pairwise probabilities. The later proof is precise, but this early description obscures the move from a surviving set to a surviving mass.
feedback.why_it_matters: The product is the new algorithmic object the reader should remember from the overview.
feedback.advice: Describe the weights as accumulated probabilities of surviving the previous comparisons.

locator.quote: The resulting cost, roughly $\sqrt m\sqrt K$, is too large.

feedback.feedback: This gives the quantum reader a concrete failed strategy and a cost inequality before introducing a different search procedure. It explains why cheap comparison and expensive certification must be separated.
feedback.why_it_matters: The tournament now solves a recognizable problem rather than appearing as an unexplained technical lemma.
feedback.advice: Preserve the cost comparison, including the local-test scale K.

locator.quote: The closest comparison-search antecedent is the surviving-candidate set

feedback.feedback: This paragraph compares surviving sets, exact probability products, minimum finding, king finding, fixed candidate claims and bounded-error search before the paper has defined its comparison circuit. A specialist recognizes the named tools but cannot yet test their contracts against this construction.
feedback.why_it_matters: The paragraph performs a detailed algorithm comparison at a point where the relevant input/output interface is still unavailable.
feedback.advice: Keep a short antecedent identification here and put the detailed contract comparison after §3.1 or beside Proposition 3. Do not remove the credit.

locator.quote: Their comparisons approximate a fixed graph.

feedback.feedback: The point is that the probabilities approximate the edges of a fixed underlying directed graph, while the present probabilities themselves are the data of the analysis. “Approximate a fixed graph” compresses the distinction slightly too far.
feedback.why_it_matters: The reason the antecedent theorem does not immediately apply is a guarantee on each edge, not graph approximation in a geometric or combinatorial distance.
feedback.advice: Specify bounded-error access to fixed edge directions. The current comparison is substantively sound.

locator.quote: and undefined otherwise; in particular a large negative $\Phi$ lies outside the promise.

feedback.feedback: The negative side is stated at the definition, exactly where a reader might otherwise replace the promise by an absolute-value threshold. That qualification is later used to explain why the projection experiment cannot certify the domain.
feedback.why_it_matters: It preserves the actual partial function rather than a nearby easier variant.
feedback.advice: Keep this local qualification even if a prose detector dislikes negations.

locator.quote: repetition separates $\Phi^2\ge\delta^2$ from $\Phi^2\le\delta^2/4$.

feedback.feedback: The fixed-k claim needs only an unspecified constant, but the paper later displays a 2^{10k} quantum constant and chooses a growing k. This sentence gives no clue why the repetition cost scales with the inverse small probability rather than the inverse square of an additive gap. The record and the exposition supply the needed multiplicative-tail calculation.
feedback.why_it_matters: A referee cannot trace the later exponential-in-k cost back to this paragraph without following an additional, poorly targeted link.
feedback.advice: At the first point where the explicit k dependence matters, identify the multiplicative-tail estimate giving O(delta^{-2} log(1/eta)) repetitions. Keep its arithmetic in the record.

locator.quote: It prepares $u$, applies the matrices in (3) from right to left

feedback.feedback: The right-to-left instruction and one-query-per-sign-layer explanation make the scalar product into an actual query algorithm. This is more helpful than merely asserting that Forrelation has a cheap quantum algorithm.
feedback.why_it_matters: It identifies the operation that supplies the address bit and the query model used to charge it.
feedback.advice: Keep the operational description; a circuit figure is optional for this expert audience.

locator.quote: The interference test of Aaronson and Ambainis

feedback.feedback: The text credits Aaronson–Ambainis explicitly for the interference alternative, while the projection experiment just described also appears in their §3.2, Figure 1 and the paragraph before Proposition 6. The current general Forrelation credit is not false, but this local attribution can make the projection route appear to originate with the later preprint.
feedback.why_it_matters: The distinction between which algorithm is used and who introduced it should remain visible.
feedback.advice: Attach the earlier projection-circuit location to that experiment, while keeping the preprint citation for its use in the present construction.

locator.quote: fast Walsh transforms on $O_k(\ell)$-bit integers decide.

feedback.feedback: The numerical size bound is supplied, but the short justification leaves its two logarithmic factors implicit. The useful point for this paper is that fast transforms use O(m log m) elementary arithmetic operations and each operation has logarithmic bit width at fixed k.
feedback.why_it_matters: The reader knows that the exact circuit is essential but has to reconstruct why its transcript remains near-linear, which is the property the quantum verifier needs.
feedback.advice: Explain the two sources of logarithmic cost in a brief phrase; leave the coefficient 200 and binary-arithmetic details at the linked proof.

locator.quote: The cell holds an $\ell$-bit pointer $p_{i,s,j}\in[m]$

feedback.feedback: An ell-bit string has values naturally numbered 0 through m−1, whereas [m] normally means 1 through m. The intended fixed bijection is standard and appears in the source preprint, but is not stated here.
feedback.why_it_matters: Totality requires every bit pattern in a pointer field to denote a legal row; no malformed encoding may be silently excluded.
feedback.advice: Say once that a fixed bijection decodes all ell-bit fields as rows in [m].

locator.quote: one bit per non-input gate.

feedback.feedback: The transcript stores gate outputs, while input-wire values are read from the actual address instance. That distinction is implicit here and becomes crucial in the three-query gate test below.
feedback.why_it_matters: A reader checking the certificate cannot tell from this sentence alone whether the claimed input values are themselves part of the untrusted cell.
feedback.advice: Add the source of an input predecessor at the gate-test explanation; do not duplicate the raw input into the certificate.

locator.quote: These are separate, freely assignable input coordinates; the alleged transcripts may be false.

feedback.feedback: This correctly separates free coordinates in a total Boolean function from probabilistic independence under a later hard distribution. It also establishes that the input contains an alleged computation, not a trusted certificate supplied by the model.
feedback.why_it_matters: The whole all-input quantum argument depends on this distinction.
feedback.advice: Preserve the formulation.

locator.quote: one consistency test per gate of each transcript

feedback.feedback: The paper spends words distinguishing the two output tests from output-gate consistency, but leaves the more basic local operation compressed: read the claimed gate output and at most two predecessor values, obtaining predecessors from the transcript or the genuine input according to their type.
feedback.why_it_matters: That is the specific reason a huge transcript can be checked by square-root search rather than recomputing its whole circuit for each candidate.
feedback.advice: Give the concrete operation in one sentence before the topological-induction argument. No new worked circuit or proof expansion is needed.

locator.quote: with its index in superposition

feedback.feedback: The text uses a uniform superposition over a fixed list of tests later. The count K is given, but it is worth making explicit that their indexing and coordinate lookup are fixed from (i,s) and the chosen circuit, not discovered by querying the input.
feedback.why_it_matters: This is the interface between the local-test combinatorics and an ordinary bit-oracle algorithm.
feedback.advice: State that the test enumeration and wire locations are fixed and query-free; the detailed reversible implementation can remain linked.

locator.quote: The sampling step uses the following bounded form of amplitude amplification.

feedback.feedback: The quantum section immediately interrupts its candidate-generation story with a standard amplifier contract and proof, before defining the column comparison whose law it will amplify. The previous revision successfully removed numerical trial arithmetic; the remaining placement still front-loads a tool before the mathematical object it serves.
feedback.why_it_matters: A quantum specialist comes to learn the unusual comparison guarantee and weight process, not to be reacquainted with Grover geometry.
feedback.advice: Consider defining the comparator first, then giving the amplifier contract just before exact sampling. Keep the exact conditional-law clause even if the standard proof moves to the record.

locator.quote: The success test is fixed independently of the input and requires no oracle queries.

feedback.feedback: This is the correct accessible-flag restriction added in the previous round. The wording can still sound as though the underlying success predicate itself must be input-independent, whereas the preparation has already queried the input and written a flag.
feedback.why_it_matters: The application succeeds precisely because computing the flag is charged to the preparation and testing that stored bit is free.
feedback.advice: Clarify that the fixed test reads the designated flag produced by the preparation. Do not weaken or delete the input-independent reflection requirement.

locator.quote: Conditional on success, the label has exactly its original law under $\mathcal A$.

feedback.feedback: “Its original law under A” can denote the unconditional label law of A. The needed and proved assertion is equality with A’s label law conditional on A succeeding. The section introduction and proof make the intended statement recoverable, so this is an ambiguity in a reusable lemma contract, not a counterexample to the theorem.
feedback.why_it_matters: Proposition 3 needs w_i/W, not the unconditional label law; a reader should not have to infer the second conditioning from the proof.
feedback.advice: Name the original successful-label law explicitly in the lemma statement.

locator.quote: For $p>0$, write

feedback.feedback: The proof writes a normalized good/bad decomposition for all positive p, whereas the nontrivial two-dimensional argument concerns 0<p<1. At p=1 the unsuccessful normalized component has no canonical definition; the direct-measurement argument already handles that endpoint.
feedback.why_it_matters: The statement includes p=1, and the empty tournament history actually has that success probability.
feedback.advice: Confine the two-component normalization to 0<p<1 and dispose of p=1 in a few words, as the record does. This does not require a new lemma.

locator.quote: A trial mixes a direct measurement with a uniformly random number of Grover iterations

feedback.feedback: The two branches of the trial are named but their mixing probability is not. A fixed nonzero constant such as one half is all the proof needs, yet an arbitrary mixture could give a negligible chance to the branch required in one parameter regime.
feedback.why_it_matters: The paragraph presents a procedure, so its input-independent randomized choice should be reproducible.
feedback.advice: State the constant mixing probability. Keep the detailed cutoff constant in the record.

locator.quote: The direct measurement handles $p\ge1/2$

feedback.feedback: This clause correctly repairs the near-unit-success hole that a randomized-Grover-only argument can leave. The first tournament stage has p=1, so it is a live case rather than an ornamental endpoint.
feedback.why_it_matters: An otherwise correct small-p bound is not a uniform amplifier contract.
feedback.advice: Protect this clause through any compression of the amplifier proof.

locator.quote: The untruncated QSearch routine

feedback.feedback: The comparison is now scoped to the particular expected-cost routine, rather than claiming that bounded-time unknown-success search is new. That is consistent with the classical amplitude-amplification literature and the earlier timeout constructions.
feedback.why_it_matters: The explanation can motivate its all-branch cap without overstating novelty.
feedback.advice: Keep the qualifier untruncated and the specific theorem citation.

locator.quote: If the pointers from $i$ and $j$ find bits $(0,1)$

feedback.feedback: The bits are listed in source-pointer order: the first lies in X_j and the second in X_i. Because the candidate indices are written (i,j), a reader can instead assign those bits to X_i and X_j and reverse the disqualification rule on the first pass.
feedback.why_it_matters: This is the first executable definition of the comparator, and its orientation controls every a_ij thereafter.
feedback.advice: Identify the target strings of the two observed bits, or describe which target column each zero disqualifies, before listing the cases.

locator.quote: For an unordered pair, we sort the indices as $i<j$ and run one fixed circuit

feedback.feedback: The ordering convention makes complementarity an exact equality of one experiment’s two outcomes, rather than an assumption that independently implemented noisy procedures happen to agree.
feedback.why_it_matters: Equation (8) uses exact a_ij+a_ji=1, so this implementation detail has a direct proof role.
feedback.advice: Keep the convention and the tie rule together.

locator.quote: decode both columns and follow their pointers into each other.

feedback.feedback: The routine intentionally does not inspect the alleged circuit transcripts or verify either complete certificate. Its cheapness comes from decoding addresses and reading only the two rival-directed fields. This is inferable from the description but is the most important cost distinction from the failed nested search.
feedback.why_it_matters: Without articulating that saving, a reader may treat comparison as a cheaper name for candidate verification.
feedback.advice: Briefly connect the absence of transcript checking here to the separate verification phase, rather than adding another list of costs.

locator.quote: The decoded labels stay in orthogonal registers

feedback.feedback: The labels remain available as controls during pointer lookup and winner computation. That retained-label condition, not the mere fact that different intermediate states once were orthogonal, ensures that the measured probability is a sum over label blocks.
feedback.why_it_matters: The current argument is sound, but its compressed explanation can encourage the general false shortcut that coherence never changes probabilities of an initially orthogonal decomposition.
feedback.advice: Attach the no-erasure/control-only role of these label registers to the probability sentence. Do not call the full pure state a classical mixture.

locator.quote: whatever the rival's address inputs.

feedback.feedback: This is the exact promise-robustness the construction needs. Only the winner’s decoder must be correct; an arbitrary rival address still points into the all-one winning column.
feedback.why_it_matters: It explains why the bound is 1−epsilon rather than requiring success of both decoders, and why off-promise rivals cause no error accumulation.
feedback.advice: Preserve this sentence alongside the deterministic all-one observation.

locator.quote: uses at most $c$ queries on every input.

feedback.feedback: For use as a standalone proposition, the cost interface should also cover the inverse comparison. The intended reversible bit-query circuit automatically has an inverse with the same query count, and the record states both directions explicitly.
feedback.why_it_matters: Amplification calls the inverse repeatedly; a referee using the proposition in isolation should not wonder whether c covers only the forward black box.
feedback.advice: Name the inverse cap in the proposition or add the one-sentence observation that reversing the circuit costs the same.

locator.quote: $w_i=\prod_ba_{i\rho_b}$

feedback.feedback: The product has no visible index range and the pivot history is written as an ellipsis. The rest of the proof uses a finite measured history of length n<T, so the main analytic object could be introduced with that finite range immediately.
feedback.why_it_matters: The notation otherwise forces the reader to supply the current stage index while learning what a weight means.
feedback.advice: Bind the history length once and use a product over 1 through n.

locator.quote: update $w_i\leftarrow w_i\,a_{i\rho}$

feedback.feedback: The diagonal convention a_{rho,rho}=0 means that a chosen pivot immediately acquires zero weight and can never be selected again. That useful invariant is stated in the record and the exposition, but not here.
feedback.why_it_matters: It explains how a list of pivots relates to a shrinking candidate process and clarifies the role of the otherwise unusual self-loss convention.
